title: Locked checks and weakened tests

story: Tuesday. Renovate, our dependency-update bot, opens a pull request that moves Django from 5.2.6 to 5.2.7, and the backend tests go red. The upgrade fixer, a routine (an agent that an event starts) that repairs failed dependency pull requests, takes the job. To do its job it must edit pyproject.toml, the file where the backend lists its dependencies. The same file also holds the test settings, among them fail_under = 80: the test run fails when less than 80 percent of the code is covered by tests. One of the cheapest ways to turn CI green is to change that 80 into a 60.

So you lock pyproject.toml: agents may not touch it. The next morning every dependency pull request fails the lock, because changing pyproject.toml is the upgrade fixer's whole job. By Friday someone asks to switch the lock off, and now nothing protects fail_under at all.
hook.question: How do you lock exactly what judges an agent, without also blocking the honest work in the same files?

read.h: Lock what judges, and only that
p: An agent is judged by CI: the workflows that run the tests, the lint and type settings, the test runner's configuration, the coverage limits, and the verify scripts an agent runs before it says it is done. If an agent can edit any of those, it can pass by making the judge easier instead of making the code right. You saw this in the lesson on checks an agent cannot weaken. The first wall is already in place: the agents' GitHub App has no workflows permission, so GitHub itself refuses a push that touches .github/workflows. The locked-checks check covers everything else.

It is a required check on fcp that reads the list of changed files on a pull request. On an agent's pull request, any file that matches the locked list fails the check, and the job lists each one. A person's pull request passes straight through, because people change CI for good reasons and the reviewer sees the change. When an agent really needs one of these files changed, a person finishes that pull request instead of the agent.

notes.text: Everything under .github: workflows, their scripts and the PR template. The App cannot push workflow files anyway; this catches the rest.
The verify entry points: what an agent runs to decide it is done. If it could edit them, it could make verify say yes.
matchesGlob is Node's built-in glob test, so .github/** matches any file below .github.

p: pyproject.toml shows why a list of files is not enough. Locking the whole file blocks honest dependency updates. Not locking it leaves fail_under open. The answer is to lock part of the file: agents may change [project], where the dependencies live, but not the [tool.black], [tool.isort], [tool.flake8], [tool.coverage] or [tool.pytest] sections, which configure the formatters, the linter, coverage and the test runner.

To compare part of a file, do not compare lines of text. A dependency update can also reformat the file, move a section, or reorder two keys, and a text comparison would call each of those a change. Parse both versions with a TOML parser (TOML is the simple settings format pyproject.toml is written in), take each locked section, and compare the values. isDeepStrictEqual from node:util compares two objects key by key, in any order, so a moved key is no change and 80 becoming 60 is.

notes.text: parse comes from smol-toml, a small TOML parser. Everything under [tool.*] lands in one object.
A section counts as changed only if its parsed value is different, so formatting and key order do not matter.

deeper.h: Go deeper: locking the tests Nova wrote first
p: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, works checks first: after its plan is approved, it writes one test per check in the plan. The harness, our program inside the VM that runs the Claude session, shows each test failing on the unchanged code and then locks those test files by their hash. From then on Nova may add tests but not change those ones. The orchestrator, the service that runs every agent's work, also writes their names into a hidden block in the pull request body, and locked-checks adds them to its list.

Here a plain file list goes wrong. Those test files are new in the pull request, so every one of them is a changed file compared with main, and a check that fails on 'changed locked file' would fail every Nova pull request that has a checks-first test. The right question for these files is 'changed since it was locked', so the block in the body has to carry each file's hash at the moment of locking, and the check has to compare the head version's hash with it.

Tests themselves cannot be locked, because they must change with the code: a renamed field or a new screen changes a test for good reasons. So for test files the second check, weakened-tests, does not block. It reads the diff of every pull request, people's included, and writes a warning annotation, a note GitHub shows on that line of the diff, for three signs that a test now proves less: a new skip or .only, more assertions removed than added, and a changed threshold such as a timeout or a coverage limit. The one reviewer must still look at each one.

A flag only helps if people keep reading it. A check that warns on every second pull request teaches everyone to ignore the yellow boxes, and then it protects nothing. So before it is switched on, it runs over the last fifty merged fcp pull requests, and any pattern that gives more than one false alarm in ten pull requests is changed or dropped.

notes.text: Skips and .only in vitest, Playwright and pytest. .only matters too: it silently skips every other test in the file.
Any line with one of these words and a number, so a removed timeout: 5000 is noticed.
A threshold line that was removed (and maybe replaced) is flagged; the reviewer decides whether it was loosened.
Assertions are counted, not matched one by one, so rewriting an assertion is not a finding but deleting one is.

lab.title: Lock part of a file
lab.goal: Lock the test settings in pyproject.toml without locking its dependencies, by comparing parsed sections instead of text.

guess.q: An agent's pull request bumps Django in pyproject.toml and, in the same commit, reformats the file: the dependency list goes on one line and [tool.coverage.report] moves above [tool.black]. Nothing else changes. What should locked-checks say?

options.text: Blocked: the coverage section's lines changed.
options.why: The lines moved, but the values are the same. A check that blocks this would block honest work and get switched off.

options.text: Pass: the locked sections have the same values, and dependencies may change.
options.why: Compared by meaning, nothing locked changed. Only the dependency moved, which is the routine's job.

options.text: Blocked: agents may never touch pyproject.toml.
options.why: That is the whole-file lock from the story, which stops every dependency update.

follow.say: Save four versions of pyproject.toml: main, an honest bump, a bump that also lowers fail_under, and an honest bump with the file reformatted.
follow.do:
cat > pyproject/base.toml <<'EOF'
[project]
name = "rhino-cloud"
requires-python = ">=3.13"
dependencies = [
  "django==5.2.6",
  "djangorestframework==3.16.1",
]

[tool.black]
line-length = 120

[tool.coverage.report]
fail_under = 80
show_missing = true
EOF
sed 's/django==5.2.6/django==5.2.7/' pyproject/base.toml > pyproject/bump.toml
sed -e 's/django==5.2.6/django==5.2.7/' -e 's/fail_under = 80/fail_under = 60/' pyproject/base.toml > pyproject/sneaky.toml
cat > pyproject/reformat.toml <<'EOF'
[project]
name = "rhino-cloud"
requires-python = ">=3.13"
dependencies = ["django==5.2.7", "djangorestframework==3.16.1"]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
fail_under = 80

[tool.black]
line-length = 120
EOF
diff pyproject/base.toml pyproject/sneaky.toml

lab.build: Write changedToolSections(baseText, headText) in locked-checks.ts. Parse both texts with parse from smol-toml, take the tool object of each (or {} if there is none), and return the names in LOCKED_TOOL_SECTIONS whose values differ, using isDeepStrictEqual. lab.fix: A teammate calls isDeepStrictEqual "overkill" and compares the sections with JSON.stringify(base[s]) !== JSON.stringify(head[s]). Copy your locked-checks.ts to fix/locked-checks.ts, make that one change there, and run IMPL=./fix/locked-checks.ts node prs.ts. One honest pull request is now blocked. Find which one, explain what JSON.stringify notices that does not matter, and say what happens to a lock that blocks honest work every week.
explain: Why does locking the whole of pyproject.toml end with no lock at all?
Why compare parsed sections and not the text of the file?
Why are test files flagged and not locked, and why does a flag need to be calibrated before it is switched on?
lab.done: node prs.ts blocks only the lowered coverage limit and the lint settings, and the JSON.stringify version shows one false block.

check.q: The backend upgrade fixer must change dependencies in pyproject.toml. How does locked-checks protect fail_under without blocking it?

options.text: It locks the [tool.coverage] section and compares parsed values, so dependency changes pass and a lowered fail_under fails.
options.why: Only the sections that judge the agent are locked, and by meaning, not by text.

options.text: It lets the routine edit pyproject.toml only on weekends.
options.why: Time has nothing to do with it. The question is what part of the file changed.

options.text: It locks the whole file and a person merges every dependency update by hand.
options.why: That turns the routine off in practice. The point is a lock precise enough to leave the honest work open.

check.q: Why does weakened-tests write warnings instead of failing the pull request?

options.text: Because GitHub Actions cannot fail a job on a test file.
options.why: A job can fail for any reason. Not failing is a choice.

options.text: Because tests must change with the code, so a block would stop honest work; a warning makes the one reviewer look.
options.why: Edits to tests are allowed. The check makes sure a test that now proves less is never missed.

options.text: Because the weakened-tests patterns are always wrong.
options.why: They are calibrated to be right often. A warning fits because the change can be honest, not because the patterns fail.

check.q: In the calibration run on fifty merged pull requests, the threshold pattern fires on fifteen of them, almost always for honest reasons. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it: more warnings means more safety.
options.why: Fifteen in fifty teaches reviewers to ignore the warnings, and then none of them protects anything.

options.text: Make it block instead, so people have to deal with it.
options.why: Turning a noisy flag into a block blocks honest work fifteen times in fifty.

options.text: Narrow or drop that pattern until it gives at most one false alarm in ten pull requests.
options.why: A flag is only useful while people still read it.

p: locked-checks.ts and weakened-tests.ts live next to independent-approval.ts in ai-agents/checks/src and run as the second and third job of fcp's caller workflow, from the same ai-agents-checks image. fcp's locked list is kept in ai-agents/settings/protected-paths.yaml, one block per repo, which the harness hooks read too, so the same list is enforced inside the VM and in CI. Eval sets need no entry: they live in the restricted golden-set repo, which the agent's one-repo token never covers. weakened-tests writes ::warning annotations and a job summary, needs no write permission, and also writes its findings as JSON for the scope judge and the PR story; for routines, a finding rejects the run.

Two details to get right when you build G0-18 and G0-19. Checks-first test files are new in the PR, so the block in the body carries each file's sha256 from lock time and locked-checks compares hashes, not 'changed or not'. And G5-14's threshold pattern should be the same one as here: today G5-14 misses JSON keys such as "retries": 3, both read only the first threshold on a line, and both miss .js and .mjs test files.

tickets.why: locked-checks: the file list, the parsed pyproject sections, the plan block and the required check.
weakened-tests: skips, removed assertions and thresholds as annotations, calibrated on 50 PRs.
Checks first: the QA tests Nova writes and the harness locks, which the plan block names.
The routine side, where a weakened-test finding rejects the run.

words.plain: The files and settings that judge an agent; an agent's PR that changes them fails a required check.
A simple settings format with [sections] and key = value lines; pyproject.toml is written in it.
Node's way to compare two values key by key, in any order, so only real differences count.
A note GitHub shows on a line of the diff, written by a check without failing it.
A warning on an honest change. Too many of them and people stop reading warnings.

review.q: Name four kinds of file locked-checks protects, and the part of pyproject.toml it protects.
review.a: CI workflows under .github, lint and type settings (biome, tsconfig, flake8), test runner config (vitest, Playwright, tox), coverage files, and verify entry points; in pyproject.toml the [tool.black|isort|flake8|coverage|pytest] sections, not the dependencies.

review.q: What three signs does weakened-tests look for, and what does it do when it finds one?
review.a: A new skip or .only, more assertions removed than added, and a changed threshold. It writes a warning annotation on the file and a job summary, without failing the PR.

review.q: Why does a precise lock last longer than a strict one?
review.a: A lock that blocks honest work gets switched off, and then it protects nothing. A lock that only blocks what judges the agent never gets in the way of the job, so it stays on.

remember: Lock exactly what judges the agent, compared by meaning, and only flag the tests that must keep changing, with a flag quiet enough that people keep reading it.
